model.box: A useful approximation of a phenomenon (simplified, but good enough to predict) — and, as this book uses it, a blueprint: a prescriptive description of a system to be built, which the built system is bound to realize.

aspects.lead: The first sense — a useful approximation
aspects.text: A simplified description prized because it predicts, not because it is exact. All models are wrong, some are useful; fidelity trades against cost, and how much fidelity you need is in the eye of the application.

A prescriptive description of the system you intend to build. A system built to a model may elaborate on it but may not diverge from it — which is what lets a model serve as an agent's marching orders.

aspects.lead: Constraint, blueprint, and knowledge base at once
aspects.text: A model handed to an agent is at once a constraint (bounding what may be built), a blueprint (saying what to build), and — because the agent reasons over it — the knowledge base for the artifact under construction.

agent.box: A controllable intelligence capable of independent reasoning over a knowledge base.

aspects.text: Given a set of constraints and a goal, it can devise a means of satisfying the goal without violating the constraints — a raven dropping pebbles to raise the water it cannot otherwise reach.

You can change its environment and the knowledge available to it and it does different things, generally following orders. Controllable means probabilistic guarantees; controlled means perfect ones. That one adjective is why governance is a major part of this book — if agents were controlled, we would not need governance at all.
It genuinely reasons in response to a query — not merely retrieving or pattern-matching stored answers.
The thing it reasons over. For this book, the models are that knowledge base — which is what ties the agent definition to the model definition.

engineering.box: The discipline of developing operable technological artifacts to solve problems, and of analytically identifying and assessing the competing means to those solutions, each with distinct trade-offs.

aspects.text: Engineering produces something that works — a technological artifact, with human operators, that addresses a real problem.

This is what separates the engineer from the technician: if you cannot articulate the trade-offs, you are not engineering. An engineer weighs competing architectures and designs against desired properties.

An engineer can model and predict the outcomes of the decisions they are about to make — from the architecture and design they propose — prior to building. Prediction-before-construction is the engineering move.

software-engineering.box: Software development produces a functioning artifact. Software engineering predictively selects a software artifact according to its desired properties.

aspects.text: Development asks "does it function and meet requirements?" Engineering asks "of the artifacts that would function, which one should we build, given the properties we want?" — and answers before building it.

aspects.lead: Why the book is about software engineering.
aspects.text: Prediction-before-construction, applied to software: choosing the artifact whose properties best serve the goal, not merely one that runs.
